summary:
Mars Outpost is an educational survival and resource-management game developed in Godot 4 for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

Players become mission commanders responsible for keeping a human outpost operational on Mars for 30 Martian sols. They must balance oxygen production, food supplies, solar energy, habitat heating, radiation protection, and crew health.

Every decision affects the base's survival. Dust storms reduce solar power, while heating and protective systems compete for limited electricity. Players can review resource forecasts, experience mission events, and learn from daily reports.

The game also includes a NASA Data Lab with an experimental connection to NASA RadLab's archived radiation observations, alongside links to other NASA educational resources.

Mars Outpost aims to make space engineering accessible and engaging for students through interactive decision-making. Its resource systems are simplified educational models rather than exact simulations of Martian conditions.
details:
Mars Outpost: Survival Mission

The Problem

Human exploration of Mars presents major engineering challenges. A sustainable habitat must provide oxygen, food, electricity, heating, and protection against radiation. These systems are interconnected, and a decision that benefits one system can create problems for another.

For students, understanding these engineering trade-offs through scientific literature alone can be difficult.

Our Solution

Mars Outpost is an interactive educational simulation that introduces students to the challenges of managing a human settlement on Mars.

The player acts as mission commander and must keep an outpost operational for 30 Martian sols.

Players control four main systems:

1. Life Support and Food Production

Players allocate operational capacity between oxygen production and greenhouse activities. Prioritizing one system limits the other.

2. Solar Energy Management

Solar panels generate electricity, but their operation involves maintenance costs. Dust storms reduce solar generation, creating additional challenges.

3. Habitat Heating

Players allocate energy to maintain safe temperatures inside the habitat. Inadequate heating can cause mission failure.

4. Radiation Protection

Players manage shelter operations to protect crew health while considering energy consumption.

Gameplay Features

The game includes:

  • A 30-sol survival campaign divided into six mission phases.
  • Resource forecasts before each decision.
  • Weather events and changing radiation hazard levels.
  • Daily mission reports and animated transitions.
  • Fictional supply and maintenance milestones.
  • Sound effects, environmental ambience, and visual alerts.
  • Multiple failure conditions and a mission-success objective.

Players must continually adjust their strategy to survive.

NASA Data and Resources

Mars Outpost includes a NASA Data Lab with an experimental integration of NASA's RadLab API.

The feature is designed to retrieve archived radiation measurements collected aboard the International Space Station.

These measurements are displayed separately from the game's simulated Martian radiation hazards. ISS observations are not used as direct estimates of radiation exposure on Mars.

The game also provides access to NASA Mars Trek, NASA's Open Science Data Repository, and educational materials from the Canadian Space Agency.

Technology

The project was developed using Godot 4 and GDScript.

It uses a 2D graphical interface, interactive resource controls, scripted simulation mechanics, audio feedback, and an HTTP request system for the experimental NASA RadLab integration.

Educational Impact

Mars Outpost aims to encourage interest in space exploration, engineering, and systems thinking.

Rather than presenting mission management as a collection of isolated tasks, the game demonstrates how energy, life support, agriculture, temperature, and crew safety interact.

Students can experiment with strategies, observe consequences, and learn from mission failures.

Scientific Limitations

The game is an educational prototype, not a scientifically calibrated NASA mission simulator.

Resource quantities, production rates, weather probabilities, and the Martian radiation hazard index are simplified gameplay parameters.

Scheduled supply events are fictional.

The project combines these educational mechanics with access to authentic NASA resources to encourage further scientific exploration.
